title: Sets
description: Python's unordered collection of unique elements, and its mathematical set operations.
objectives: Create sets and understand their uniqueness guarantee
Use union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference

content.heading: Sets and Membership
content.body: A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable elements, written with curly braces: {1, 2, 3} (an empty {} creates a dict, not a set — use set() for an empty set). Adding a duplicate value has no effect; sets automatically discard duplicates. add(x) inserts a single element; update(iterable) inserts every element from another iterable; remove(x) deletes an element (raising KeyError if it's absent); discard(x) does the same but silently does nothing if absent. Because sets are unordered and implemented with a hash table internally, membership testing (x in my_set) is on average much faster (O(1)) than for a list (O(n)).

content.heading: Set Algebra
content.body:
Sets directly support the classic mathematical set operations: union (a | b or a.union(b)) — all elements in either set; intersection (a & b or a.intersection(b)) — elements in both; difference (a - b or a.difference(b)) — elements in a but not b; symmetric difference (a ^ b) — elements in exactly one of the two sets. issubset() and issuperset() (or <=/>=) test containment relationships between sets.

Because a plain set is mutable, it cannot itself be an element of another set or a dictionary key (it isn't hashable). For that case, Python provides frozenset, an immutable variant of set that supports all the same read-only operations but no add/remove.

content.code:
a = {1, 2, 3}
b = {2, 3, 4}
print(a | b)          # {1, 2, 3, 4} union
print(a & b)          # {2, 3} intersection
print(a - b)          # {1} difference
print(a ^ b)          # {1, 4} symmetric difference

tags = set(["python", "python", "java"])
print(tags)           # {'python', 'java'} — duplicate discarded
content.explanation: The set constructed from a list with a duplicate 'python' entry automatically deduplicates. Set algebra operators mirror the mathematical operations directly.

keyPoints: Sets store unique, hashable elements with no guaranteed order
Membership testing in a set is typically much faster than in a list
frozenset is an immutable, hashable set usable as a dict key or set element
commonMistakes: Writing {} expecting an empty set (it creates an empty dict instead)
Assuming sets preserve insertion order (they don't — dicts do, since Python 3.7, but sets don't guarantee it)
Trying to put a plain (mutable) set inside another set or use it as a dict key
